Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Rafael, a thirty-three-year-old physical therapist of South Eastern Asian descent, experienced the life-threatening accident on a Tuesday morning when a delivery truck struck his sedan at forty miles per hour. The impact drove his shoulders back, the seatbelt locking across his chest while a sharp, metallic groan filled the cabin. To Rafael, the moment held its shape in his memory: the bent steering wheel, the bruising pressure along his ribs, the sudden stillness after the noise. In the weeks that followed, he began waking with dream residue, his sheets twisted around his legs as he sat up from nightmares, still certain the frame had buckled beneath him. Unwanted thoughts arrived without warning, pulling his attention back to the scuff marks on the dashboard, the angle of his own stiffness, the exact pitch of the collision. When loud noises echoed from traffic or clinic doors slamming shut, he found himself easily startled, his shoulders lifting as if bracing for another strike. As days folded into months, Rafael’s daily routine settled into a series of deliberate patterns. He noticed weapons in every environment, his eyes catching on the heavy kettle in his kitchen, the metal leg of a waiting-room chair, the clinical scissors on his desk, all of them suddenly capable of causing harm. You can never know who will harm you, he reasoned, and the thought settled alongside his other observations. He began checking his surroundings constantly, pacing the aisles of his rehabilitation clinic, running his fingers along the equipment racks, ensuring nothing was loose or misplaced. Worst case rehearsal became a quiet, ongoing practice; before starting a treatment session or even stepping into his car, he would mentally walk through the scenarios, mapping exits, weighing the distance between himself and potential hazards. His concentration grew fractured. While guiding a patient through a stretching routine, he would lose his place mid-sentence, his gaze drifting to the rolling stools, the ceiling tiles, the door handles, as if waiting for something to give. He had come to believe his body had been permanently damaged by what happened, and he was certain that his own physiology would no longer operate without betrayal. The compulsion to clean and organise grew into a concrete anchor in his life. Rafael found himself wiping down the therapy mats three times before a session, rearranging the resistance bands by thickness, and straightening the pamphlet stands in the clinic’s waiting area. The repeated motions coexisted with his other habits rather than replacing them. Across the dinner table, his wife learned to step carefully when he was mid-rehearsal, attuned to the rhythm of his scanning eyes and the way he would pause before answering a question, his mind already holding the worst possibility. His work reflected the same accumulation of habits; colleagues noted his deliberate pace, his hands lingering on equipment longer than necessary, his treatment plans occasionally delayed by the extra minutes spent confirming the room was secure. His PCL-5 profile registered at thirty-eight, a quiet tally of these coexisting patterns. Now, sitting across from a therapist, Rafael reports the same relentless loop. The loud noises of traffic still pull him back to the crash site, and the intrusions arrive whether he is walking through a crowded clinic corridor or sitting in the stillness of his home. He has stopped driving after dusk, not because of fear of the road itself, but because the sudden brake lights and the echo of metal on metal feel like previews of another impact. What frightened him most was the unreliability of his own body, the sense that the same injury could happen again at any moment, and what he hoped for was a way to quiet the constant rehearsal, to trust that his ribs would hold and his legs would carry him without sudden failure. He came to the clinic seeking a way to navigate the vigilance, hoping to find a rhythm where the world could move without demanding he brace for it.
